overview: A closure is a function value that remembers (captures) variables from the lexical scope in which it was defined, keeping them alive and accessible even after the enclosing function has returned.
Anonymous functions are function literals written inline with no name (`func(...) {...}`); a closure is simply an anonymous (or named) function that references variables from its surrounding scope.

Captured variables are shared by reference, not copied by value — every closure over the same variable observes and mutates the same storage, which the Go runtime moves to the heap via escape analysis when needed.
learningObjectives: Write anonymous function literals, assign them to variables, and immediately invoke them (IIFE).
Build stateful closures (counters, accumulators, generators) and reason about which variables they capture and share.
Explain capture-by-reference, escape analysis, and why a closed-over variable is heap-allocated.
Diagnose and fix the loop-variable capture bug, including how Go 1.22 changed per-iteration loop variable semantics.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A closure is a record storing a function together with an environment: a mapping of the free variables of the function (variables used locally but defined in an enclosing scope) to the storage locations they were bound to when the closure was created.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: An anonymous function is a function without a name that you can write inline. When that function uses a variable from the function around it, it 'closes over' that variable — it keeps a live link to it, so the variable survives and stays shared even after the outer function has returned.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Closures originate from lambda calculus and were popularized by Lisp and Scheme in the 1970s, where the term 'closure' (Peter Landin, 1964) described a function paired with its environment. Go adopted first-class functions and closures from the start (Go 1.0, 2012), following the tradition of languages like Scheme and Smalltalk, and made them central to idioms such as defer, the functional options pattern, and sort.Slice less-functions.

whyItMatters.business: Closures power configuration APIs (functional options) used by SDKs like AWS and gRPC, letting libraries evolve without breaking callers — protecting product velocity and backward compatibility.
whyItMatters.engineering: They enable callbacks, middleware, decorators, and lazy generators with minimal boilerplate, keeping behavior local to where it is used instead of scattered across types.
whyItMatters.scalability: Closure-based middleware chains and per-request handlers let a single binary compose cross-cutting concerns (auth, logging, rate limiting) that scale uniformly across thousands of requests.
whyItMatters.cost: Encapsulating small bits of state in a closure avoids defining whole struct types and methods, reducing code volume and maintenance cost.
whyItMatters.reliability: Used correctly, closures localize state and reduce global mutable variables; used incorrectly (loop capture, unsynchronized sharing across goroutines) they are a top source of subtle production bugs.

coreComponents.name: Function literal (anonymous function)
coreComponents.definition: An expression `func(params) results { body }` that produces a function value with no declared name.
coreComponents.purpose: Define behavior inline where it is used — as an argument, return value, or immediately invoked expression.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Carry executable code; optionally reference variables from the enclosing scope, turning it into a closure.
coreComponents.examples: double := func(x int) int { return x * 2 }

coreComponents.name: Captured (free) variable
coreComponents.definition: A variable used inside the function literal but declared in an enclosing scope.
coreComponents.purpose: Give the closure persistent, shared state that outlives the enclosing call.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Hold state by reference; the same storage is observed by the closure and the enclosing scope.
coreComponents.examples: count is captured by the returned func in makeCounter

coreComponents.name: Escape analysis
coreComponents.definition: A compile-time analysis that decides whether a variable can live on the stack or must be moved to the heap.
coreComponents.purpose: Allow captured variables to outlive the stack frame that created them, safely and automatically.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Detect that a variable escapes via a closure/return/pointer and heap-allocate it.

internalWorking: When the compiler sees a function literal that references a variable from an enclosing scope, it records that variable as a captured (free) variable of the closure.

Escape analysis determines whether the captured variable can stay on the stack; if the closure outlives the enclosing frame (e.g., it is returned or started in a goroutine), the variable is allocated on the heap instead.
The closure value is represented at runtime as a pointer to a small struct: the function's code pointer plus pointers to the captured variables' heap cells.
Because the closure holds a pointer to the variable (not a copy), reading or writing the variable inside the closure operates on the same storage the enclosing scope used — capture is by reference.

Multiple closures created in the same scope that capture the same variable all point to that single cell, so they observe each other's mutations; each fresh call to the enclosing function allocates a new, independent cell.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: enclosing func runs --> declares variable v --> defines func literal referencing v --> compiler marks v captured --> escape analysis: v escapes? --> heap-allocate v --> build closure {code ptr, &v} --> return/pass closure --> closure called later --> dereferences &v --> reads/writes the SAME v
dataFlowWalkthrough: makeCounter() is called; the runtime allocates the local variable count (which escapes) on the heap and initializes it to 0.
Inside makeCounter, a func literal `func() int { count++; return count }` is created; it captures &count.
makeCounter returns the closure value; its stack frame is gone but count survives on the heap because the closure references it.
The caller invokes the closure: it dereferences &count, increments it to 1, and returns 1.
A second, independent call to makeCounter() allocates a brand-new count cell, so the two counters never share state.

keyTerminology.meaning: A function value bundled with the captured variables from its defining scope.
keyTerminology.importance: The mechanism that gives anonymous functions persistent, shared state.

keyTerminology.meaning: A variable referenced inside a function but declared in an outer scope.
keyTerminology.importance: Free variables are exactly what a closure captures; identifying them tells you what state is shared.

keyTerminology.meaning: Closures hold a pointer to the variable, not a snapshot, so they see later mutations.
keyTerminology.importance: Explains both the power (shared state) and the danger (loop-capture and goroutine bugs) of closures.

keyTerminology.meaning: Immediately Invoked Function Expression — a func literal called the instant it is defined: `func(){...}()`.
keyTerminology.importance: Useful for scoping, one-shot initialization, and deferring computed cleanup.

importantConcepts.concept: Capture is by reference, not by value
importantConcepts.explanation: A closure stores a pointer to the variable. If the variable changes after the closure is created, the closure sees the new value. To freeze a value, copy it into a new variable (e.g., a parameter or `v := v`) that the closure captures instead.
Each invocation of an enclosing function creates a fresh set of captured variables. Two counters from two makeCounter() calls are fully independent because each call allocated its own count cell.

importantConcepts.concept: Closures and goroutines/defer interact via timing
importantConcepts.explanation: A closure run later (in a goroutine or deferred) reads captured variables at call time, not definition time. This is why a deferred closure sees the final value of a loop variable and why goroutines must copy values they need to snapshot.

variationsAndTypes: Stateful generators/accumulators: makeCounter, ID generators, running totals held in a captured variable.
Higher-order returns (decorators/middleware): functions that take a function and return a wrapped function (e.g., logging or auth middleware in net/http).
Functional options: variadic `...Option` where each Option is a closure mutating a config struct (gRPC, AWS SDK, uber-go/zap).
Inline callbacks/predicates: func literals passed to sort.Slice, strings.Map, http.HandleFunc, or filepath.WalkDir.
advantages: Encapsulate small bits of mutable state without declaring a whole struct and methods.
Enable concise callbacks, predicates, and middleware that live next to their use site.
Support flexible, backward-compatible APIs via the functional options pattern.
Allow lazy evaluation and deferred computation by capturing the inputs and running later.
disadvantages: Capture-by-reference causes subtle bugs (loop variable, shared state across goroutines) that are hard to spot.
Captured variables escape to the heap, adding allocation and garbage-collection pressure on hot paths.
Long-lived closures can unintentionally keep large captured objects alive, causing memory leaks.
Heavy use of nested closures can hurt readability and make stack traces and debugging harder.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: For callbacks, predicates, middleware/decorators, functional options, and small encapsulated state that does not warrant a named type.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: When the captured state is large or long-lived (prefer a struct with explicit fields), on allocation-sensitive hot paths, or when shared mutable capture across goroutines would require careful synchronization.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: A closure is like a backpack a worker carries away from the office: the worker (the function) keeps a live reference to the shared whiteboard (the captured variable) back in the room. Even after the meeting (enclosing function) ends, the worker can still read and update that exact whiteboard. Two separate meetings produce two separate whiteboards — but two workers from the SAME meeting share one whiteboard, so each sees the other's edits.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A closure captures a copy of the variable's value at the time it is defined.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It captures the variable itself (by reference); it sees later changes, and the value read is whatever the variable holds when the closure runs.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Anonymous functions and closures are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: An anonymous function is just a function with no name; it becomes a closure only when it references variables from an enclosing scope.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Closures are slow and always allocate.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only captured variables that escape are heap-allocated; a func literal that captures nothing (or only stack-safe values) can avoid heap allocation entirely, as escape analysis decides.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Closure-based middleware composes cleanly across thousands of requests, but watch for per-request closures that capture large objects and inflate allocations under load.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Avoid sharing captured mutable state across goroutines without synchronization; prefer passing snapshots as arguments to eliminate races.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Use deferred closures (with recover) at boundaries, remembering they read captured variables at the moment they run, not when registered.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Profile heap allocations with pprof; closures that escape large variables show up as allocation hot spots and can be refactored.
productionConsiderations.security: Be careful capturing secrets/credentials in long-lived closures, as they remain reachable in memory; clear or scope them tightly.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: On hot paths, replacing escaping closures with explicit structs or passing values by argument can cut GC pressure and CPU cost.
productionConsiderations.performance: Use `go build -gcflags=-m` to see escape decisions; avoid creating closures in tight inner loops when a top-level function would do.

codeExamples.title: Stateful counter closure with independent instances
codeExamples.overview: makeCounter returns a closure that captures a private count variable; two counters maintain fully independent state.
codeExamples.breakdown: Each call to makeCounter() declares a new local `count` initialized to 0 and returns a func literal that closes over it. Because the returned closure references `count`, escape analysis moves `count` to the heap so it survives after makeCounter returns. Every call to the closure increments and reads the same cell, so state persists across calls. Crucially, `a` and `b` come from two separate makeCounter() invocations, so they capture two distinct `count` cells — calling b() returns 1 while a is already at 3, proving the counters are independent.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Expecting `b` to continue from `a`'s value (it won't — different cells). Declaring `count` as a package-level global by mistake would make all counters share one variable.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: If you need many counters on a hot path, a small struct with an int field and an Inc() method avoids per-counter heap allocation of the captured variable and is easier to inline.

codeExamples.title: The loop-variable capture bug and the Go 1.22 change
codeExamples.overview: Demonstrate why closures over a loop variable historically printed the final value, the two classic fixes, and how Go 1.22 changed the semantics.
codeExamples.breakdown: Before Go 1.22 the `range` loop reused a single variable `it` across all iterations; closures capture by reference, so by the time the goroutines ran (after the loop finished) they all read the last value, commonly printing "c c c". Go 1.22 changed loop semantics so that `for` loop variables are scoped per iteration — each iteration gets its own `it`, eliminating the bug for code compiled at language version go1.22 or later. The two explicit fixes work on every version: `it := it` creates a fresh per-iteration variable that the closure captures, and passing `it` as the argument `v` copies the value at goroutine-launch time so nothing is captured by reference. The arg form is often preferred because the copy is explicit and obvious to readers.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
buggy-on-old-go: a
buggy-on-old-go: b
buggy-on-old-go: c
shadow-fix: a
shadow-fix: b
shadow-fix: c
arg-fix: a
arg-fix: b
arg-fix: c
(within each block the order may vary; on Go < 1.22 the first block could print c c c)
codeExamples.commonIssues: Assuming the bug is gone everywhere — it only goes away when the module's go directive is go1.22+. Mixing the diagnosis: the loop variable, not the closure body, is the shared thing.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Prefer passing the value as an argument: it documents intent, is version-independent, and lets the compiler reason about a plain copy instead of an escaping captured variable.

codeExamples.title: Functional options pattern (closures as configuration)
codeExamples.overview: A widely used Go idiom where each option is a closure that mutates a config struct, giving extensible, backward-compatible constructors.
codeExamples.breakdown: Each `WithX` function returns an `Option`, which is a closure capturing the arguments passed to WithX (here `d`). NewServer starts from sensible defaults and applies each option closure to the server in order, so later options can override earlier defaults. Because new behavior is added by writing new `WithX` functions, existing call sites never break — this is why gRPC, the AWS SDK, and uber-go/zap use this pattern. The closures capture only their parameters (copied by value), so there is no shared-mutable-state hazard.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting to set defaults before applying options, or relying on option order when options conflict. Capturing a shared external variable in an option (instead of a parameter) can introduce surprising aliasing.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Keep Option closures tiny and side-effect-free except for mutating the config; for very hot constructors, a plain config struct passed by value can avoid the slice and closure allocations.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: An HTTP API needs cross-cutting concerns — request logging, authentication, and panic recovery — applied uniformly to many handlers without duplicating code in each one.
endToEndExample.inputData: Incoming HTTP requests to handlers like /orders and /users, plus a set of middleware functions, each `func(http.Handler) http.Handler`.
endToEndExample.architecture: A middleware chain built from closures: each middleware is a higher-order function that captures the `next` handler and returns a new handler that wraps it, composed left-to-right around the final business handler.
processingSteps: Define each middleware as a function that takes the next http.Handler and returns a closure (http.HandlerFunc) capturing `next`.
Compose middlewares into a chain helper that folds them around a base handler.
Wrap the business handler with recovery (outermost), then logging, then auth.
On each request, the closures run in order: recover defers a recover(), logging records start/stop, auth validates the token before calling next.
The innermost business handler executes only if every preceding closure called next.
endToEndExample.output: Every route automatically gets logging, auth, and panic recovery with a single wrapping call, and handlers stay focused on business logic.
endToEndExample.monitoring: The logging closure emits per-request method, path, status, and latency; the recovery closure increments a panic counter metric.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: The recovery middleware's deferred closure catches panics and writes a 500; the auth closure short-circuits with 401 and never calls next on failure.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Cross-cutting behavior is defined once as closures and composed declaratively, so adding a new concern means writing one middleware, not editing every handler.

industryUseCases.problem: Dial and server constructors need dozens of optional, evolving settings without breaking existing callers.
industryUseCases.solution: The functional options pattern: grpc.DialOption / grpc.ServerOption values are closures that mutate internal config (e.g., grpc.WithTransportCredentials).
industryUseCases.benefits: Backward-compatible API growth, readable call sites, and defaults that callers override only as needed.

industryUseCases.problem: Apply cross-cutting concerns (logging, auth, recovery) across many handlers.
industryUseCases.solution: Middleware as higher-order functions returning closures that capture the next handler, composed into chains.
industryUseCases.benefits: Reusable, composable request pipelines without per-handler duplication.

industryUseCases.company: AWS SDK for Go v2 & uber-go/zap
industryUseCases.problem: Configure clients and loggers with many tunables while keeping constructors stable.
industryUseCases.solution: Variadic functional options (closures over their parameters) plus closures passed to sort.Slice for ordering results.
industryUseCases.benefits: Extensible configuration, clear defaults, and inline comparators without defining sort.Interface types.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Closure-based middleware and per-request handlers scale cleanly, but profile per-request closures that capture large structs; converting them to handlers that reference shared, read-only state reduces allocation under high QPS.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Recovery middleware uses a deferred closure with recover() at the request boundary; remember deferred closures read captured variables at execution time, so capture request context before the deferred body may need it.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Compose graceful-shutdown logic as closures that capture a context and drain in-flight work, ensuring no request-handling closure is interrupted mid-flight during rollout.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Keep option/middleware closures idempotent and side-effect-free except for their intended config mutation, so replays or restarts reapply them safely.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Use `go build -gcflags=-m` to confirm which captured variables escape; hoist closures out of tight loops and prefer passing values as arguments to avoid heap-allocating captured loop variables.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Escaping closures add GC pressure; on hot paths replace stateful closures with explicit structs/methods to cut allocations and reduce CPU and memory cost.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Avoid capturing long-lived secrets (tokens, keys) in closures that outlive their need, since captured variables remain reachable in memory; scope them tightly and zero them when possible.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Have logging/metrics middleware closures emit structured fields (trace ID, latency, status) so every wrapped handler is observable without extra code.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Validation predicates passed as closures (e.g., to filter or map) should be pure functions of their inputs to remain testable and free of hidden captured state.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Recovery and logging closures should log captured request identifiers and alert on panic-rate and latency thresholds derived from middleware metrics.

recommendedPractices: Pass loop and per-iteration values as arguments to closures rather than capturing them, even on Go 1.22+, to make copies explicit.
Keep closures small and prefer pure functions of their captured/passed inputs.
Use the functional options pattern for constructors with many optional, evolving settings.
Reach for a named struct with methods when captured state is large, long-lived, or shared across many call sites.
engineeringStandards: Run tests with the -race flag when closures share state across goroutines.
Use `go build -gcflags=-m` in performance reviews to surface unexpected escapes.
Document which variables a returned closure captures and mutates.
designRecommendations: Make middleware closures composable: take and return the same type (e.g., http.Handler).
Prefer capturing by argument over capturing shared external variables to avoid aliasing surprises.
namingConventions: Name option constructors WithX (WithTimeout, WithTLS) and the option type Option.
Name middleware by the concern they add (LoggingMiddleware, RequireAuth), not generic names.
documentationStandards: State whether a closure captures by reference and what its lifetime is.
Note any closure that must not be shared across goroutines without synchronization.
testingStrategies: Unit-test closures by exercising the returned function multiple times to verify state persistence and independence.
Test that two independent factory calls produce non-shared state.
Use the race detector for closures launched in goroutines.

commonMistakes.mistake: Capturing a loop variable in a closure (especially in a goroutine) on Go < 1.22.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The loop variable was a single shared variable, and closures capture by reference.
commonMistakes.impact: All closures observe the final iteration value (e.g., 'c c c'), causing wrong results or duplicated work.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Pass the value as an argument or shadow it with `v := v`; upgrade the module to go1.22+ for per-iteration variables.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a closure captures the value at definition time.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Mental model from value-copy languages; forgetting capture is by reference.
commonMistakes.impact: The closure reads a later, unexpected value when it finally runs.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Copy the value into a new variable or parameter that the closure captures to freeze it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Long-lived closure capturing a large object, preventing GC.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The captured variable stays reachable as long as the closure does.
commonMistakes.impact: Memory leak; large buffers or caches are never freed.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Capture only the small fields you need, or set the captured reference to nil when done.

commonMistakes.mistake: Sharing a mutable captured variable across goroutines without synchronization.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Closures make sharing implicit and easy to overlook.
commonMistakes.impact: Data races and corrupted results (detected by -race, can crash in production).
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Pass copies as arguments, or guard the shared variable with a mutex/atomic/channel.

comparisonSection.explanation: Closures are concise for small/short-lived state; structs are clearer and cheaper for large, long-lived, or widely shared state.

comparisonSection.optionB: C++ lambdas ([=] by value, [&] by reference)
comparisonSection.explanation: Go always captures by reference; to capture a value you must copy into a new variable, whereas C++ lets you choose per-capture.
Go 1.22 scopes loop variables per iteration, eliminating the classic capture bug that older versions exhibited unless you copied the variable.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between an anonymous function and a closure?
beginnerQuestions.answer: An anonymous function is a function literal with no name. It becomes a closure only when it references variables from its enclosing scope, capturing them.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Tests the precise distinction many candidates blur.

beginnerQuestions.question: How do you immediately invoke an anonymous function in Go?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Append a call to the literal: `func(){ ... }()` — an IIFE. You can also assign it to a variable first and call that.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Checks basic syntax fluency with function literals.

intermediateQuestions.question: Does a Go closure capture variables by value or by reference, and why does it matter?
intermediateQuestions.answer: By reference — it holds a pointer to the variable, so it sees later mutations and shares storage with the enclosing scope. To freeze a value you copy it into a new variable the closure captures.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Tests the core semantic that underlies most closure bugs.

intermediateQuestions.question: Why is a variable captured by a returned closure allocated on the heap?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Because the closure outlives the enclosing stack frame; escape analysis detects the variable escapes and heap-allocates it so it remains valid.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Probes understanding of escape analysis and memory model.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain the loop-variable capture bug and what Go 1.22 changed.
advancedQuestions.answer: Before Go 1.22 the loop variable was shared across iterations; closures capturing it all saw the final value. Go 1.22 makes loop variables per-iteration (at language version go1.22+), so each closure captures its own copy and the bug disappears. Explicit fixes (`v := v` or passing as an argument) work on all versions.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Tests up-to-date language knowledge and the underlying cause.

advancedQuestions.question: How can closures cause memory leaks, and how do you prevent them?
advancedQuestions.answer: A long-lived closure keeps every variable it captures reachable, so a captured large object or buffer is never collected. Prevent it by capturing only the minimal data needed, copying small values, or nil-ing captured references when finished.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A worker spawns one goroutine per item in a slice using a closure, and on the team's older Go toolchain every goroutine processes the last item repeatedly.
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Goroutines run after the loop body; if the closure captures the shared loop variable by reference, all of them read its final value. The fix is to give each goroutine its own copy.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Pass the item as an argument to the goroutine func (or shadow with `it := it`), and/or upgrade the module's go directive to go1.22+ which scopes loop variables per iteration. Verify with the race detector and a test asserting all items were processed.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a configurable client constructor for a library used by many teams, where new options are added frequently without breaking existing callers.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Use the functional options pattern: define `type Option func(*config)` and `WithX` constructors that return closures capturing their parameters; the constructor starts from defaults and applies each option.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Options are extensible and backward-compatible but add small allocations and indirection; a plain config struct is faster but less ergonomic and harder to evolve compatibly.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Keep options pure and order-independent where possible; for hot constructors offer a fast-path config struct, and document precedence when options overlap.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: A closure is an anonymous (or named) function value that captures variables from its enclosing scope by reference, keeping them alive and shared.
keyConcepts: Anonymous func: func(args) results { body }; call inline as an IIFE with trailing ().
Capture is by reference — closures see later mutations of captured variables.
Captured variables that escape are heap-allocated via escape analysis.
Each enclosing-call creates fresh captured variables; closures from the same call share them.
formulas: closure value ≈ {code pointer, pointers to captured variables}
commands: go build -gcflags=-m main.go    # show escape-analysis decisions
go run -race main.go            # detect races on captured shared state
go vet ./...                    # flags some loop-capture mistakes
interviewPoints: Anonymous function != closure; closure = function + captured environment.
Go captures by reference; copy to freeze a value.
Captured escaping variables live on the heap.
quickNotes: Pass loop values as arguments to be safe on every Go version.
Long-lived closures can leak large captured objects.
Functional options = closures mutating a config struct.

keyTakeaways: An anonymous function becomes a closure when it captures variables from its enclosing scope; Go always captures by reference, so closures share and see later mutations.
Captured variables that outlive their stack frame are moved to the heap by escape analysis, which is why a returned closure's state persists across calls.
Each call to an enclosing function creates independent captured state, but closures created together share the same variable — the root of the loop-capture bug fixed per-iteration in Go 1.22.
Closures power core Go idioms — callbacks, middleware/decorators, and the functional options pattern — but require care with goroutine sharing, escapes, and long-lived captures in production.
